query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the traditional EAM reference in TOR-TILD with a deep neural network (DNN) potential trained on ab initio configurations for both solid and liquid phases of multicomponent high‐entropy alloys will improve the reference–target phase‐space overlap and reduce the thermodynamic‐integration path mismatch.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (with five or more principal elements) in both their solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures.
generation.intervention: Develop and employ a DNN-based interatomic potential as the reference model for thermodynamic integration instead of conventional EAM potentials. The DNN potential should be trained on ab initio data that extensively sample the various atomic configurations present in the liquid and near-melting conditions.
generation.conditions: Applicable for alloys exhibiting high melting points (typically refractory HEAs, e.g., equiatomic compositions such as TiZrTaHfNb-derived systems or other systems with similar configurational complexity) at temperatures near or just below their melting points.
generation.structural_mediator: The DNN potential, by being trained on a broad set of atomic configurations, mediates a more accurate mapping of the free-energy landscape. This improves the phase-space overlap by better capturing the many-body interactions and configurational entropy in the ab initio liquid state.
generation.mechanism: By covering a more diverse range of atomic environments than EAM, the DNN potential substantially reduces the discrepancies between the reference and target systems along the thermodynamic integration path. This enhanced accuracy is expected to lower the integration path mismatch because the potential energy surface used in the integration better reflects the true ab initio landscape.
generation.predicted_outcome: A statistically significant reduction (potentially on the order of >30% improvement, although the precise magnitude remains uncertain) in the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s traditional EAM reference approach.
generation.baseline: The current measure of integration path mismatch or free-energy errors obtained using TOR-TILD's EAM references across the relevant temperature range in high-entropy systems.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be most effective in high-melting, compositionally complex alloys where traditional EAM potentials fail to capture the liquid state’s many diverse atomic configurations. Its performance for lower-melting or less complex systems remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work using DNN potentials in similar systems (e.g., carbonitrides in high-entropy materials) supports the idea that neural network potentials can better sample diverse configurational space, the exact quantitative reduction in thermodynamic integration mismatch is not yet firmly established.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a benchmark high-entropy alloy system (e.g., a refractory equiatomic HEA). Perform two sets of thermodynamic integration free-energy calculations: one using the standard TOR-TILD approach with an EAM reference and the other using the DNN-based potential as the reference. Ensure that both calculations sample a similar range of atomic configurations at temperatures near the melting point. The experiment should statistically compare the free-energy integration paths in terms of variance and absolute mismatch to ab initio computed free energies.
measurements: Free-energy difference along the integration path for both methods.
Statistical variance and deviation of the integration path from ab initio target values.
Quantitative measure of phase-space overlap (e.g., distribution overlap metrics) between reference and target configurations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DNN-based potential does not produce a statistically significant reduction in the free-energy integration path mismatch (e.g., less than a 30% improvement or within measurement error) compared to the EAM reference, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition. The improved melting behavior of high-entropy compounds by the addition of nitrogen provides a promising way towards modification of thermal properties of functional and constructional materials.

It is important to consider that the metal carbide precursors have very strong covalent/ionic bonds, and are therefore enthalpy stabilized. However, the same might not be the case for their mixture. In fact, a statistical analysis of the AFLOW.org enthalpies indicates that the gain in formation enthalpy by adding mixing species, ΔHf(N + 1) − ΔHf(N), decreases with N, and can easily be overcome by the monotonic increase in entropy-gain for the disordered systems (to go from order to complete or partial disorder). In the AFLOW analysis, the threshold between low- and high-entropy systems is around four mixing species. To have completely entropy-stabilized materials, five mixing species are required (similar to the Entropy-Stabilized Oxides). For carbides in which only the metal-sublattice is randomly populated, five metals should be enough to achieve carbide entropy stabilization, especially at equi-composition. Notably, if other sublattices were also allowed to contain disorder, (e.g., reciprocal systems like TaxHf1−xC1−y,), then the overall number of species might reduce.
